summary: Lit in October 1820 at the southwest end of Galloo Island in Lake Ontario; automated in 1963; the tower is now privately owned and closed.

structures.note: Present tower; the first tower of 1820 was rebuilt in 1866-67. Rowlett gives 55 ft (16.5 m); LighthouseFriends gives sixty feet; the USLHS place record gives 54.75 ft.

access.note: Privately owned. LighthouseFriends: grounds, dwelling and tower closed. USLHS archive: Open to Public: No.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends says a light maintained by the Coast Guard remains in the tower)

events.note: Congress appropriated $12,500 for a lighthouse on Galloo Island (3 March 1819)
Dwelling and tower built under contract by Elisha Ely
First exhibited 4 October 1820 (clipping file: 'Established in 1820')
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed in the tower
Congress appropriated $15,000 for repairs and renovations (7 April 1866)
New tower and dwelling completed; begun late 1866 (Rowlett: 'Tower 2' dated 1867)
Steam fog signal practically completed on 30 June 1897; authorized by act of 11 June 1896 per the 1897 report (the 1893 report cites an act of 15 February 1893)
Assistant keepers' dwelling rebuilt; earthen sewer pipes laid
Gray limestone tower painted white in March 1902 (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper Graves towed a small power boat four miles after it ran out of fuel (24 August)
Keeper Graves reached a father and son's motorboat in a squall and rescued both men and a trunk (LighthouseFriends)
19 April: Graves and Assistant Keeper Frazier towed the disabled power boat Louis Donald (10,500,000 minnows aboard); LighthouseFriends dates it 18 April
Assistant Keeper William E. Frazier towed the disabled power boat Glinda, two men aboard, to Grenadier Island
Air diaphone replaced the steam whistle (LighthouseFriends)
Light electrified; characteristic changed to a group of three flashes every twelve seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Head keeper Robert C. Graves retired 1 June 1933 after 40 years of Government service
Power changed from direct to alternating current; a line to the Coast Guard boat station let its crew run the light and fog horn by remote control
National Register of Historic Places (per LighthouseFriends; the NRHP nomination PDF was not digitised when checked)
Coast Guard declared the station surplus
GSA auction of the tower; four bids opened 27 September 2000; winning bid $87,654 from a private buyer (not named)
Rowlett's directory: inactive since 2011; LighthouseFriends says a Coast Guard light still operates in the tower (sources disagree)
Island bought by new private owners, apparently including the light station property (Rowlett's directory; owners not named here)

corrections.why: The record's tower dates to 1820 but the standing tower is the 1866-67 rebuild: the clipping file reads 'Rebuilt in 1867', Rowlett lists the present tower as 'Galloo Island (2) 1867', and LighthouseFriends describes the new tower begun late in 1866. The 1820 tower was replaced.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Rowlett's directory gives 'station established 1829'. The clipping file ('Established in 1820') and LighthouseFriends (first exhibited 4 October 1820) agree on 1820, which the record keeps. The 1829 event is treated as Rowlett's error, not a second opening.

The Light-House Board's 1893 report gives an act of 15 February 1893 authorizing the signal; the 1897 report gives an act of 11 June 1896 and says it was practically completed on 30 June 1897. The story reports both and does not choose.

notes_for_editor: Galloo Island, fact-check of 2026-10-27. All 77 original evidence quotes were found in their cached sources on the first run. Changes made: lead 'Congress paid for it' changed to 'appropriated money'; standing tower finished 1867 (begun late 1866); Platt cited by his full name to LighthouseFriends (the clipping reads 'C. T. Platt'); fiscal-year titles for the 1893, 1897 and 1899 Light-House Board reports (the 1893 volume's heading reads 'Fiscal year ended June 30, 1893'; the 1899 heading reads 'Fiscal year ended June 30, 1899'); the 1897 entry cited by item 1191 in place of 'no page index'; the 1899 sewer sentence now matches the report's 'Earthen pipe sewers leading from both keepers' dwellings'; 'the shore was already moving' and 'the fog signal came late' removed as interpretation; the Platt surge is now quoted rather than paraphrased; the auction wording follows LighthouseFriends ('the property', 'not included in the auction'); the 1915 rescue is LighthouseFriends' 'most courageous rescue'. Rowlett's 2022 sale of the island (apparently including the light station) is added to Today without naming the owners. Unresolved: the 2011 deactivation (Rowlett) and LighthouseFriends' statement that a Coast Guard light still operates in the tower conflict; the story leaves it open. Name variants: 'Willie E.' (1919 Commissioner list) against 'William E.' (1921 report and roster). The 1919 Commissioner list was matched by table position (the station name follows the names in the OCR); the archive.org page image was viewed in the browser pane at a resolution too low to read the names, so the spelling is not confirmed from the image. The 1919 Lighthouse Service Bulletin (p.23) independently places Graves and an assistant keeper Frazier at Galloo Island for the 19 April rescue, which supports the list. F. Byron Johnson: USLHS 1876-1906 against LighthouseFriends 1877-1906. Graves: the 1933 notice says he entered the Lighthouse Service as keeper in February 1903; USLHS has him first assistant 1903-1906. The 1919 rescue date: the Bulletin gives 19 April, LighthouseFriends 18 April. Tower height: USLHS gives 54.75 ft to the lantern centre; Rowlett 55 ft (16.5 m); LighthouseFriends sixty feet; the story gives the last two. The 1893 Light-House Board report is 'fiscal year ended June 30, 1893'; the act of 15 February 1893 falls in that fiscal year. The NRHP nomination for Galloo (83001682) is a 'not yet digitized' placeholder on NPGallery; the 1983 listing rests on LighthouseFriends. The Rowlett page names the 2022 owners and the LighthouseFriends page names the 2000 bidder; neither is named in the story (living private owners). LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: facts paraphrased, with short quotations only. The 1838 Platt report is an OCR'd clipping compilation; its quotations are kept as OCR'd. Not used, for the editor: the 1916 Bulletin (p.43) has a motor boat blown ashore near the Galloo light station; it could be added if read in full.
